claims.text: Nanoscale grain-boundary density and distribution govern nucleation of the magnetostructural transition in FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys.
The relevant nanoscale grain boundaries are created during deposition.
Controlled post-deposition annealing can refine the grain structure.
Annealing-induced grain refinement increases the density of interfacial nucleation sites.
Increasing interfacial nucleation-site density smooths the first-order magnetostructural transition.
Smoothing the transition reduces transition sharpness and hysteresis.
The as-deposited alloy has an ordered, single-phase hexagonal state.
The as-deposited alloy has a large, sharp, and hysteretic magnetocaloric response.
Annealing at roughly 350–450 °C can induce grain refinement without triggering secondary-phase formation.
An intermediate-temperature anneal can promote a nanostructured grain-boundary network while preserving the ordered hexagonal structure.
Enhanced grain-boundary density provides more nucleation sites for the magnetostructural transition.
Additional grain-boundary nucleation sites lower transition energy barriers.
Lower transition energy barriers produce a more gradual transition and reduce hysteresis.
A finer internal microstructure improves the alloy's surface-to-volume ratio.
The proposed microstructural refinement supports faster heat exchange during magnetic-cooling cycles.
Annealed samples will exhibit a broader and more gradual magnetostructural transition than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will exhibit lower hysteretic losses than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing may shift the transition temperature and trade peak entropy change against reversibility.
Overall magnetocaloric performance under low-applied-field cycles will improve after annealing.
Annealing outside the grain-refinement window may cause grain coarsening, secondary phases, increased hysteresis, or phase instability.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is explicitly bounded to annealing conditions that avoid secondary-phase formation, but the falsification rule treats secondary-phase formation as falsifying the mechanism. Secondary phases would instead show that the intervention fell outside its stated validity domain unless refinement was independently achieved and tested.

The mediator is internal grain-boundary density and grain size, whereas the heat-exchange explanation invokes improved surface-to-volume ratio. Refining internal grains does not by itself increase the specimen's external surface-to-volume ratio, so this heat-transfer link is internally mismatched.
